Ichthyology is the branch of science — specifically a branch of zoology — that is dedicated entirely to the study of fish.

That one sentence is the heart of it, but let's unpack what that truly means.

When ichthyology says "fish," it doesn't just mean the goldfish in your bowl or the salmon on your plate. It covers all fish across three major groups:

  • Bony fish (like tuna, cod, clownfish, trout) — the largest group, covering over 30,000 known species
  • Cartilaginous fish (like sharks, rays, and skates) — whose skeletons are made of cartilage, not bone
  • Jawless fish (like lampreys and hagfish) — ancient, eel-like creatures without proper jaws

So ichthyology spans an enormous range of creatures — from a tiny transparent minnow in a mountain stream to a great white shark in the open ocean.

An ichthyologist (the person who practises ichthyology) doesn't just identify fish and give them names. The field is much broader. Ichthyologists investigate:

  • Anatomy and physiology — How is a fish's body built? How do its organs work? How does it breathe underwater using gills?
  • Behaviour — How do fish hunt, mate, communicate, or school together in groups?
  • Ecology — Where do fish live, and how do they interact with other animals, plants, and their environment?
  • Evolution — How did different fish species develop over millions of years? Which species are related to which?
  • Classification (taxonomy) — Naming, describing, and categorising every fish species in a structured, scientific way
  • Distribution — Which fish are found in which rivers, lakes, seas, or oceans, and why?
  • Reproduction — How do fish breed, lay eggs, or give birth?
  • Physiology under extremes — How do some fish survive in freezing Antarctic waters, or in deep-sea environments with crushing pressure and total darkness?
Where does ichthyology sit among the sciences?

Ichthyology is a sub-field of zoology (the study of animals), which is itself a branch of biology (the study of life). It overlaps heavily with:

  • Marine biology — but marine biology covers all ocean life (whales, corals, jellyfish, etc.), whereas ichthyology focuses specifically on fish, whether they live in the sea, in rivers, or in lakes
  • Ecology — when ichthyologists study how fish fit into their ecosystems
  • Genetics — when they study DNA to understand fish evolution or relationships between species
  • Palaeontology — when the fish being studied are fossils of long-extinct species

So ichthyology is specialised, but it regularly borrows tools and methods from many other sciences.
Why does ichthyology matter in the real world?

This is not just an academic curiosity. Ichthyology has deep, practical importance:

  • Fisheries and food supply — Much of the world's population depends on fish as a primary source of protein. Ichthyology helps scientists understand fish populations, how fast they reproduce, and whether they are being overfished — knowledge that directly informs fishing laws and quotas.
  • Conservation — Hundreds of fish species are endangered or threatened. Ichthyology tells us which species are at risk, why, and what can be done to protect them.
  • Medicine — Some fish produce compounds used in medicines. Studying them closely has led to breakthroughs in treatments for various diseases.
  • Aquaculture (fish farming) — To farm fish effectively and sustainably, you need to know how they grow, feed, breed, and get sick. All of this comes from ichthyology.
  • Understanding ecosystems — Fish are a central pillar of most aquatic food webs. When fish populations collapse, entire ecosystems can unravel. Understanding fish is understanding the health of rivers, lakes, and oceans.
  • Pollution monitoring — Fish are often used as biological indicators. If fish populations in a river start dying or changing behaviour, it can be an early warning signal that the water is being polluted.

There are approximately 34,000–35,000 known species of fish — more than all species of mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians combined. And scientists estimate there are still many species yet to be discovered, especially in deep oceans and unexplored river systems in tropical regions. This makes ichthyology one of the richest, most active areas of biological research in the world.

Ichthyology is, in short, the complete, rigorous, scientific study of fish — their bodies, behaviour, evolution, classification, habitat, and relationship with the rest of the living world. It is both a pure science (driven by curiosity and the desire to understand nature) and an applied science (with real consequences for what we eat, how we protect nature, and how we manage the planet's water bodies).

If you ever hear the word used in a sentence — "She has a doctorate in ichthyology" or "The museum's ichthyology department houses thousands of fish specimens" — it simply points to this specialised, fish-focused corner of biology.
